nowplaying-cli

nowplaying-cli is a macOS command-line utility for retrieving currently playing media, and simulating media actions.

Use nowplaying-cli to get song information and play/pause your media through an easy to use CLI!

Disclaimer: nowplaying-cli uses private frameworks, which may cause it to break with future macOS software updates.

Tested and working on:

Ventura 13.1

Usage

nowplaying-cli <cmd>
command description
get [propName1 propName2 … ] get now playing media properties
get-raw get all non-nil now playing media properties in dictionary format
play play the currently playing media regardless of current state
pause pause the currently playing media regardless of current state
togglePlayPause toggle play/pause based on current state
next skip to next track
previous go to previous track

The aim of the study is "To investigate the impact of sales promotion strategies on Nigeria Breweries Limited’s performance, exploring factors influencing their effectiveness, ethical considerations, and their contribution to the organization’s sustainable success and competitive advantage". 
The objectives are "To determine the impact of sales promotion strategies on Nigeria Breweries Limited's financial performance, measured by changes in revenue, profit margins, and market share, over a period of three years; To evaluate the ethical considerations associated with sales promotion strategies in Nigeria Breweries Limited, using a framework based on corporate social responsibility principles and guidelines; To investigate potential innovative sales promotion techniques within the beverage industry, benchmarking against competitors and best practices over the period of 3 months;  To develop a comprehensive training program for Nigeria Breweries Limited’s marketing and sales teams, focused on implementing effective and ethical sales promotion strategies". 
The rationale of the study is below
The use of sales promotion strategies, a wide range of tactics and techniques designed to stimulate customer interest and increase sales of products or services, has become increasingly important for organizations as they seek to improve their performance in today’s highly competitive business environment (Kotler et al., 2017). The proposed study seeks to explore the effect of sales promotion strategies on the overall performance of Nigeria Breweries Limited (NBL), a leading brewing company in Nigeria’s beverage industry. The research is of great significance due to the ever-growing competitive landscape of the beverage industry, where companies compete on several fronts, including product quality, branding, and promotional activities. It aims to fill an existing knowledge gap by evaluating the effectiveness of sales promotion strategies and their ethical implications, consequently providing actionable insights on adopting innovative tactics and training programs.
From a theoretical perspective, this research will draw on marketing theories. The consumer behavior theory, according to Hanaysha (2016), posits that individuals and groups make consumption decisions based on their needs, preferences, and the perceived values of available options. The stimulus-response theory, on the other hand, contends that consumers will react to a promotional stimulus, such as discounts or freebies if the perceived results align with their needs and elicited affect. Finally, the hierarchy of effects model explores how promotional campaigns can progress consumers through various stages, from awareness to action. This study will also be guided by the resource-based view (RBV) of the firm, which posits that a company’s resources and capabilities are the primary determinants of its competitive advantage and performance (Barney, 1991). According to the RBV, a company can gain a sustainable competitive advantage by leveraging its unique resources and capabilities to create value for its customers and stakeholders. These theories will offer invaluable frameworks to analyze the effectiveness of various sales promotion strategies adopted by NBL. In the organizational context, Nigeria Breweries Limited presents a suitable case study, as it operates in a highly competitive industry with numerous local and global competitors. Assessing the organization’s promotional activities could uncover opportunities to refine, innovate and enhance their sales and marketing effectiveness. Additionally, NBL has a responsibility to uphold ethical and sustainable practices, which adds another layer of relevance to this research. The potential interest in this study is wide-ranging, as it could be beneficial for marketing professionals, educators, and policymakers. Marketing professionals may apply the study’s findings to their strategies to drive organizational performance, while educators can incorporate the research in their curriculum to better equip future marketing practitioners. Policymakers, on the other hand, may use the study to understand the industry’s best practices and establish suitable legal and ethical frameworks. The personal interest in this study stems from the desire to contribute to the advancement of marketing knowledge, specifically in the context of the Nigerian brewing industry, and enhance my understanding of promotional strategies’ effectiveness and ethical implications. By conducting this research, I hope to offer valuable insights that promote sustainable success and competitive advantage for organizations such as Nigeria Breweries Limited.

∂y/∂t = f(y, x) + D∇^2y

where f(y, x) and g(y, x) are the reaction terms describing the population growth and the information density, respectively, and D and C are the diffusion coefficients for the population and the information density. The Laplacian operator (∇^2) represents the diffusion of the respective variable in space.

For the reaction terms, we can use a logistic growth model for the population:

f(y, x) = ry(1 - y/K)

where r is the intrinsic growth rate, K is the carrying capacity (maximum population density), and y/K is the effect of density-dependent regulation on the population growth.

For the information density term, we can use a linear model:

g(y, x) = ax

where a is a constant that determines the effect of information density on population growth.

Solving for the steady-states of the system (when ∂y/∂t = 0 and ∂x/∂t = 0) gives:

y = K

x = 0

This means that the population reaches its maximum density at the carrying capacity when there is no information in the environment. This is because there is no regulation of the population growth, so it grows until it reaches the available resources.

On the other hand, when there is a high density of information in the environment, the population density is lower and more stable. The behavior of small perturbations around this equilibrium depends on the diffusion coefficients, D and C. If D is much larger than C, the population is more diffusive and can respond more quickly to changes in the environment. If C is much larger than D, the information density is more diffusive, and changes in the environment may take longer to affect the population density.

Overall, this model suggests that the presence of information in the environment can regulate population growth, and the analysis of steady-states and perturbations can reveal important insights about the behavior of the system.

To perform a linear stability analysis, we need to assume that the population growth is near some stable equilibrium point, in which case small perturbations around the equilibrium point will grow or decay exponentially. We can write the equation above as:

where ∇² is the Laplacian operator for the concentration and f(x) is a non-linear function describing the growth of the population in terms of the substance concentration.

where f'(x0) is the derivative of the function f(x) evaluated at the equilibrium point x0. The term D∇²ε(x) is the diffusion term while f'(x0)ε(x) is the linearized reaction term.

If f'(x0) < 0, the system is stable and any perturbations will decay exponentially, whereas if f'(x0) > 0, the system is unstable and perturbations will grow exponentially.

x = x* + δx

where Δ = ∂^2/∂x^2 + ∂^2/∂y^2 is the Laplacian operator.

This is a homogeneous equation with constant coefficients, which can be solved by assuming solutions of the form exp(kx), leading to a characteristic equation:

D^2k^4 + (2D^2AC - 2Dk^2)k^2 + ACD^2 = 0

This equation can be factored to yield the eigenvalues:

λ = ±ik^2, where k^2 is a root of the quadratic:

k^4 + (2AC/D)k^2 + C/D = 0

We can solve for the roots using the quadratic formula:

k^2 = (-2AC/D ± sqrt((2AC/D)^2 - 4(C/D))) / 2

k^2 = -AC/D ± sqrt((AC/D)^2 - C/D)

Since k^2 is real and positive, the square root can be written as a real number, and the eigenvalues are given by:

λ = ± i√k^2

λ = ± i√(-AC/D ± sqrt((AC/D)^2 - C/D))

These are the main results of the linear stability study. The sign of the real part of the eigenvalues determines the stability of the steady state solution. If the real part is negative, the perturbations decay and the steady state is stable. If the real part is positive, the perturbations grow and the steady state is unstable. If the real part is zero, further analysis is needed, because the perturbations neither grow nor decay.
To perform a linear analysis, we assume that the variables y and x are small perturbations around a steady state solution, such that y = y* + δy and x = x* + δx, where y* and x* are the steady state values. Substituting these expressions into the partial differential equations and neglecting terms of order higher than δy and δx yields:

∂δy/∂t = ry(1 - y/K)*δy + D∇^2(δy)

∂δx/∂t = ay δx + C∇^2(δx)

We can now use the method of separation of variables to find solutions of the form δy(x, t) = Y(x)*T(t) and δx(x, t) = X(x)T(t). Substituting these into the equations above and dividing by YT yields:

(1/T)dT/dt = ry*(1 - y/K) + D*(Y''/Y)

(1/T)dX/dt = ay* + C*(X''/X)

Since the left-hand sides are functions of t only, and the right-hand sides are functions of x and y, we can set them equal to a constant λ to obtain two ordinary differential equations:

d^2Y/dx^2 + (λ/D)*Y = 0

d^2X/dx^2 + (λ/C - ay)*X = 0

These are Sturm-Liouville equations, whose solutions depend on the boundary conditions. For simplicity, we assume periodic boundary conditions on a one-dimensional interval of length L, such that Y(L) = Y(0) and X(L) = X(0). The general solutions are:

Y(x) = Asin(kx) + Bcos(kx)

X(x) = Cexp(-sx) + Dexp(sx)

where k = sqrt(λ/D) and s = sqrt(λ/C - ay). The constants A, B, C, and D can be determined from the boundary conditions.

We now impose the condition that the eigenvalue λ must be real and negative for stability. This means that the solutions δy and δx must decay exponentially in time, and any small perturbations must be damped out. From the equations above, we see that λ/D and λ/C - ay must both be positive for this condition to hold.

Therefore, the eigenvalues λ are given by:

λ = n^2 π^2 D/L^2, n = 1, 2, 3, ...

for the population density, and

λ = (s^2 + ay) C

for the information density.

For stability, we require that λ < 0. The first condition is always satisfied, since D, L, and n^2 are positive. The second condition becomes:

s^2 + ay < 0

Since s^2 > 0, this requires ay < 0, which means that the sign of a and y* must be opposite. In other words, if the information density has a positive effect on population growth (a > 0), then the steady state population density must be below the carrying capacity (y* < K). Conversely, if the information density has a negative effect on population growth (a < 0), then the steady state population density must be above the carrying capacity (y* > K).    

Therefore, the system is stable if the information density has a negative effect on population growth (a < 0), or if the effect is positive but the population density is below the carrying capacity (y* < K). If the effect is positive and the population density is above the carrying capacity (y* > K), the system is unstable and prone to oscillations or even population crashes.

Terminology
State Variables
In a dynamical system (such as an Initial Value Problem), the dependent variables are also called the state variables. e.g., in Problem 5 of HW #9, x and v (or ẋ) are the state variables. These variables are often put into an array, which is called the state array. While the independent variable (usually time, for us) is not technically considered a state variable, we are primarily interested in the system state as a function of time. In our case, we will insert the independent variable as the first value in the state array and call it the augmented state array.

Mode Shapes and Natural Frequencies
Consider the vibration system below. As a two degree of freedom system, it has two natural frequencies and two mode shapes. If the two masses are both displaced to the left (by the correct distances) and released, they will each undergo perfect sinusoidal motion. Both will oscillate at the same frequency – called the first natural frequency. The first mode shape is a normalized vector representing respective signed amplitudes of their oscillations. The second mode shape and second natural frequency occur when the two masses are released after being displaced (by the correct distances) in opposite directions. In this case, the values in the mode shapes will have different signs, because the masses are moving in opposite directions.

Task #1
Write a single function script to perform the Third Order Adams-Bashforth-Moulton algorithm on a system of ordinary differential equations (IVP). The program must be able to handle any number of differential equations (an IVP with any number of state variables).
Your function m-file will receive through its header the following problem parameters (in this
exact order):
a. a cell array containing the function handles of the equations describing the time derivatives of the several state variables
b. the initial augmented state-array – a numerical row array containing the needed starting values of the independent variable and the several state variables (in the same order as the function handles in the cell array from the first input argument)
c. the step size to be used, and
d. the number of steps to take

Function Output
Your file should not return anything to the calling program. Instead, it should
i. print to screen (the command window) the final state of the system, including t, and

Store only the final result of each time step, not the predicted or non-converged corrected values. Title each plot ‘Var1’, ‘Var2’, etc. Try help plot and help title in the MATLAB command window to learn more about plotting. num2str will also be useful for creating the labels themselves.

Hints for your Function Script
Handling a System of Un-predetermined Size
Technical
Because you will not know in advance the order of the IVP your function will be asked to solve, some of the system parameters will need to be passed in as arrays, rather than as scalars. The step size and number of steps will still be scalars, but there will be an un-predetermined number of state variables, each of which will have an associated starting value and derivative expression. The starting value of each state variable is a scalar, so the collection of them can be stored in a normal array. On the other hand, your function script must be passed a separate function handle for the equation for the time derivative of each state variable. To store function handles, we must use a cell array. So then, you must be able to evaluate a function handle stored in a cell array. We did this in Lab #4, but I cover it again later in this document.
NOTE: Because your augmented state array will include time as the first value, the function stored in the nth index of the cell array is actually the derivative of the state variable in the (n+1)th index of the augmented state array.

Metaphysical
To figure out how to structure your code to deal with any size system, consult HW#9 and the notes from lab. In the HW, we performed RK3 on a 2nd order system. We can call the state variables x and v, and we can call their slopes (time derivatives) k and m, respectively. Feel free to write out and logically group the steps you took to solve the system for one timestep. Now, imagine we have 3 or 4 state variables each with their own slopes. Again, write out and logically group the steps you took to solve the system of equations. What changed about the process? Did the number of groups increase? Did the number of steps within particular groups increase? Now, we need to replace the RK3 algorithm steps with the ABM3 algorithm steps. Pay careful attention to the following differences:
a. the predictor and its modifier are performed once per time step, the corrector and its modifier are repeated until convergence each time step
b. the is no modifier on the predictor in the first time step
c. when performing the modifier steps, you use only non-modified values
d. when you check for convergence you compare only modified values

Function handles with unknown number of inputs
If you remember doing this for Modified Secant on a system of equations, then you may skip this section.
Up to now, you’ve probably only used function handles for equations that had a predetermined number of inputs. For this program, each derivative equation may be a function of the independent variable and any or all of the state variables. This is only a problem because you don’t know now (as you’re writing the function script) how many or which of the state variables will appear in each of the derivative equations. Fortunately, MATLAB allows us to put arrays into the equation function evaluation.
For example, if I define a function handle:
d1_by_dt = @(t,a) a(1) * a(3) / (2 + t);
when you ask MATLAB to evaluate the mathematical expression, MATLAB will expect to receive a scalar as the 1st argument, and an array of at least three terms as the 2nd argument. It will use the first and third terms in the array, along with the scalar, to evaluate the expression.
The augmented state array passed into the function already has t as the first value, so let’s just stick with that. Then our example equation becomes:
d1_by_dt = @(a) a(2) * a(4) / (2 + a(1));
You, of course, will have no prior knowledge of which state variables are used in each derivative expression. Therefore, for each derivative evaluation, you will need to submit an array containing the correct values of the dependent variable and all of the state variables, in the same order as the initial values in the passed-in augmented state array. When grading your code, it will be my responsibility to ensure that all of the derivative equations use the correct variables.

Function handles in cell arrays
The function handles of the derivative expressions of the several state variables will be passed to your function script in a cell array. The syntax for evaluating a function handle that is stored in a cell array is as follows:

• array_name is the name of the cell array in which the handles are stored
• n is the index into the cell array, in which is stored the expression for (d/dt)y n
• input1 thru inputQ are the inputs to the mathematical expression represented by the function handle – in our case that will simply be the augmented state array
Please note that those are braces around the index ‘n’ and parentheses around the arguments.

The ABM3 process
To calculate the predicted value of each state variable, you are going to perform very similar math:

Take advantage of how MATALB deals with vectors to simplify the process of calculating the predictor for all the state variable and each subsequent corrector for all the state variables. Create an array that holds the g m evaluations for all of the state variables. You will have 3 or 4 of these, one for each timestep. Then you can ...

INTRODUCTION
In recent times, environmental concerns have turned to be a focal point for both consumers and businesses  likewise. Accordingly, there's a growing emphasis on green marketing strategies by companies that offer environmentally friendly products. This research aims to explore the impact of green marketing on consumer buying behavior in the manufacturing industry in Nigeria. The study focuses on how consumers’ appreciations of green products and marketing practices, as well as their motivations,  impact their buying behavior in the Nigerian market.   
Green marketing involves promoting environmentally friendly products and services that contribute to sustainable practices. As environmental consciousness continues to accelerate encyclopedically, businesses worldwide are espousing green marketing strategies to attract customers and gain a competitive edge. Nigeria, with its fast- growing population and expanding economy, represents a significant market for eco-friendly products. Still, the relationship between green marketing and consumer buying behavior in Nigeria has not been considerably studied. Thus, this research is  pivotal for companies operating in or looking to enter the Nigerian market, as it examines factors that  impact consumers’ decisions to buy eco-friendly products. Such insights can be capitalized on by companies to develop further effective marketing strategies aimed at compounding their market share and enhancing customer  fidelity. Also, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on sustainable business practices and consumer adoption of green products by providing insights specific to the Nigerian context, making it relevant to researchers, marketers, and policymakers concerned with environmental issues and sustainable consumption patterns.   
The literature review provides an overview of existing knowledge on green marketing and its impact on consumer buying behavior, highlighting gaps that this research aims to address. The theoretical framework and research questions guiding the  research are also introduced. The methodology used in this project is described and justifications are furnished for the choice of research design, sampling, and data collection techniques. The limitations of the research design are also addressed, and remedies to overcome them are suggested. The next section presents the findings of the study, including the analysis of research data and a comparison of the findings with the literature reviewed earlier. Incipiently, concluding remarks sum up the  crucial findings and their contribution to the existing body of knowledge on green marketing and consumer buying behavior. Furthermore, research limitations are identified, suggestions for coming studies are offered, and the practical implications of the findings are discussed. 


REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE
Evaluation Of The Existing Body Of Knowledge On The Issue
Green marketing refers to the promotion of products and services with environmentally friendly features, contributing to sustainable development and practices (Peattie & Crane, 2005). Companies have been adopting green marketing strategies in response to the growing environmental consciousness of consumers and the demand for products that align with their eco-friendly values (Rahbar & Wahid, 2011). Green marketing strategies can also provide a competitive edge and foster positive brand associations, resulting in increased consumer loyalty and market share (Chen, 2010). In the context of the manufacturing industry, green marketing strategies encompass a variety of initiatives, such as using eco-friendly materials, energy-efficient production processes, recyclability, and minimizing waste generation (Rahbar & Wahid, 2011). Manufacturers that adopt green marketing strategies often experience enhanced brand reputation, improved consumer loyalty, and increased market success, demonstrating the importance of this approach in today’s sustainability-driven world (Chen, 2010; Peattie & Crane, 2005).

An essential determinant of the success of green marketing initiatives is consumers’ perceptions and awareness of green products (Nguyen et al., 2020). According to the Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen, 1991), an individual’s behavior is preceded by their intentions, which are influenced by their attitudes towards the behavior, the relevant subjective norms, and the perceived control they have over performing the behavior. Consequently, positive consumer attitudes and increased awareness of the benefits of green products and practices are critical to translating these attitudes into actual purchase behavior (Biswas & Roy, 2015; Chen, 2020). However, research has identified a gap between pro-environmental attitudes and the actual adoption of green products, which can stem from factors such as lack of information or ineffective green marketing communication, leading to consumer skepticism or greenwashing (Biswas & Roy, 2015; Nguyen et al., 2020). As such, effective communication through green marketing campaigns is crucial to bridge the gap between consumers’ favorable attitudes towards green products and their actual purchase behaviors (Leonidou, 2019).

Environmental concerns have also become increasingly relevant in driving consumer buying behavior, with many consumers considering the ecological implications of their purchase decisions (Dangelico & Vocalelli, 2017). These concerns have led to a willingness from consumers to pay a premium for green products, which in turn has created an opportunity for businesses to cater to this demand (Dangelico & Vocalelli, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2020). Environmental concerns are predominantly driven by factors such as ecological crises, global climate change, and heightened awareness of the environmental repercussions of unsustainable production and consumption (Chen, 2020; Dangelico & Vocalelli, 2017). As such, manufacturers must recognize the significance of environmental concerns in shaping consumer purchasing behavior and strategically position their green products to capitalize on this emerging trend (Dangelico & Vocalelli, 2017). While the existing literature offers an understanding of the impact of green marketing and consumer perception on eco-friendly product adoption, most studies have been conducted in developed countries, where environmental issues may be more pronounced (Nguyen et al., 2020). Thus, there is a need for research focusing on the impact of green marketing on consumer buying behavior in developing nations, such as Nigeria. Factors such as cultural, economic, and regulatory conditions can influence the translation of pro-environmental attitudes into actual purchase behaviors and warrant further exploration.

Theory of Planned Behaviour
The Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) has been widely used in understanding and explaining various human behaviors, including those related to green consumption (Ajzen, 1991). This study applies TPB as the theoretical underpinning to investigate the influence of green marketing on consumer buying behavior in the Nigerian manufacturing industry. According to TPB, intentions play an essential role in shaping individuals’ behavior, and these intentions are influenced by three key factors: attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control (Ajzen, 1991). Attitudes refer to the evaluation of the behavior, which may be positive or negative, subjective norms represent the cultural and social pressures an individual perceives in performing the behavior, and perceived behavioral control signifies the individual’s beliefs about their ability to effectively perform the behavior (Ajzen, 1991). The TPB has been successfully applied in previous studies to examine consumer behavior regarding environmentally friendly products and practices (e.g., Biswas & Roy, 2015; Leonidou et al., 2013). These studies have found that positive attitudes towards environmentally friendly products and practices, in conjunction with favorable subjective norms and higher perceived behavioral control, lead to stronger intentions to adopt green products and engage in eco-friendly behavior.

In the context of this study, TPB can be employed to explore how consumers’ attitudes towards green products, the influence of social and cultural norms, and their perceived ability to engage in eco-friendly purchasing behavior interact to shape their intentions and ultimately their adoption of green products in the Nigerian manufacturing industry. By employing the Theory of Planned Behavior as the foundational framework, this study aims to gain a deeper understanding of the complex factors affecting the impact of green marketing on consumers’ purchase behavior while accounting for the specific cultural, economic, and social influences unique to Nigeria.

Research Questions and Hypotheses 
Building upon the existing literature and utilizing the Theory of Planned Behavior, this study aims to address the following research question in the context of the Nigerian manufacturing industry:
RQ: How does green marketing influence consumer buying behavior in the Nigerian manufacturing industry?

To better understand the relationship between green marketing and consumer buying behavior, the following specific research hypotheses have been developed:
H1: Positive consumer attitudes towards green products and their marketing practices enhance the likelihood of purchasing eco-friendly products in Nigeria.
H2: The influence of subjective norms, such as social and cultural pressures, can significantly affect the relationship between green marketing and consumer buying behavior in Nigeria.
H3: Higher perceived behavioral control over engaging in eco-friendly purchasing behavior strengthens the positive impact of green marketing on consumer buying behavior in Nigeria.

By addressing these hypotheses and investigating the research question, this study aims to reveal the intricate interplay of factors affecting the impact of green marketing on consumer buying behavior in Nigeria, while considering the cultural, economic, and social context unique to the country.



METHODOLOGY
Identification of paradigm
This study adopts a positivist paradigm, which seeks to formulate precise and quantifiable explanations based on observable empirical evidence (Creswell, 2014). Utilizing a positivist approach allows for the measurement of objective reality through numerical data, providing a scientific and empirically grounded understanding of the impact of green marketing on consumer buying behavior in the Nigerian manufacturing industry context. The adoption of quantitative methods aligns with the positivist paradigm, ensuring that the research outcomes are comparable and generalizable across populations and contexts (Bryman, 2016)

Justification of Chosen Methodology and Methods
Research Design
The decision to employ a cross-sectional survey design for this study is grounded in its ability to efficiently collect data from a large and diverse sample of participants (Bryman, 2016). This design enables the exploration of relationships between green marketing, consumer attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and purchase behavior within the Nigerian manufacturing industry. The cross-sectional approach also allows for the simultaneous examination of multiple variables, providing valuable insights into the intricate interplay of factors affecting consumer buying behavior in response to green marketing initiatives (Creswell, 2014).

Data Collection
To capture a representative sample of the Nigerian population’s perspectives, a self-administered online questionnaire is used as the primary data collection method. This data collection approach allows for efficient and cost-effective access to a geographically diverse sample while offering participants the convenience and flexibility to complete the questionnaire at their own pace (Bryman, 2016). The questionnaire will consist of closed-ended questions, utilizing Likert-scale items to measure respondents’ attitudes towards green products, the influence of subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and eco-friendly purchase behaviors. This allows for the numerical measurement of participants’ responses, which can be analyzed statistically to determine the relationships between variables (Creswell, 2014). Additionally, the questionnaire will include demographic questions (e.g., age, gender, education, and income), ensuring that the analysis can account for potential variations in consumer behavior based on different population groups. Such demographic information promotes a more nuanced understanding of the factors shaping green marketing’s impact on consumer buying behavior in the Nigerian context (Bryman, 2016).

Sampling
A stratified random sampling technique is employed to ensure a representative and diverse sample drawn from the Nigerian population. This sampling strategy involves dividing the population into distinct and non-overlapping groups or strata based on geographical regions within Nigeria. Participants are then selected randomly from each stratum, resulting in a balanced representation of responses from different areas of the country (Creswell, 2014). By ensuring a geographically diverse sample, this study can account for potential variations in green marketing’s effectiveness and consumer behaviors based on regional differences (Bryman, 2016).

Data Analysis
The data collected through the online questionnaire will be analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS). Descriptive statistics (e.g., means, standard deviations) will be calculated to present a summary of respondents’ demographic characteristics and their responses to the Likert-scale items. Inferential statistical techniques, such as multiple regression analysis, will be employed to test the research hypotheses and assess the relationships between green marketing, consumer attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and eco-friendly purchase behavior (Creswell, 2014). This comprehensive data analysis approach allows for a robust understanding of the phenomenon under investigation and contributes to the evidence base for green marketing’s impact on consumer buying behavior in developing countries like Nigeria.

Limitations of the Research Design and Potential Remedies
Despite the efficiency and strengths of cross-sectional survey designs, certain limitations need to be acknowledged. First, the self-reported nature of the data may be influenced by social desirability bias, leading participants to overstate their environmentally conscious behaviors (Bryman, 2016). To mitigate this bias, phrasing of questionnaire items should encourage honesty and minimize social desirability influence.

Second, the cross-sectional design does not allow for the establishment of causality between variables, as it captures a snapshot of the population at a particular point in time (Creswell, 2014). However, utilizing the Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen, 1991) provides theoretical justification for the expected relationships between variables. To explore causal relationships further, future research could employ longitudinal designs to examine changes in consumer behavior and green marketing interventions over time.

Third, the study’s generalizability may be limited due to the specific focus on the Nigerian manufacturing industry. While the findings will undoubtedly provide valuable insights into the Nigerian context, caution should be exercised when attempting to generalize the results to other industries or countries (Bryman, 2016). Researchers may consider extending the investigation to other industries or countries to explore the broader applicability of the findings.



RESULTS
Presentation & Discussion of the Analysis of the Research Data
The data collected through surveys and interviews were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics to understand the impact of green marketing on consumers’ buying behaviour in the Nigerian manufacturing industry. The analysis of the data focused on three thematic codes to delve deeper into the constituents of the said impact – green awareness, attitudes, and purchase behaviour.

Initial descriptive statistics provided a general overview of the demographic profile of the participants, which included their age, gender, educational background, and environmental concern. The results indicate that a majority of participants hold a positive attitude towards the environment showcasing their heightened interest in green initiatives, products, and practices (Smith & Brower, 2012). Findings also depicted that higher-educated consumers exhibited a greater inclination towards sustainable options, corroborating earlier studies in the context of green marketing (Biswas & Roy, 2015).

Subsequently, inferential statistics, such as regression analysis, were employed to assess the relationship between green marketing practices and consumer buying behaviour. The analysis revealed a significant positive relationship between consumers’ perception of green products and their intention to purchase sustainable products (Guagnano, Stern, & Dietz, 1995). Although green marketing strategies were identified as a crucial factor in influencing consumer choices, other factors like cost, product availability, and perceived product quality were also identified to be influential factors (Joshi & Rahman, 2015).

To draw inferences from the data collected, thematic codes derived from the literature review were used. The first theme - green awareness - surfaced as an essential component in driving consumer behaviour in the Nigerian manufacturing industry. The study found that effective green marketing could lead to an increase in consumer awareness and, consequently, promote sustainable consumption (Hamid et al., 2018). This indicates the need for manufacturing companies to invest in educational and promotional campaigns that highlight their green initiatives to target and influence their prospective customer base effectively.

The second theme - attitudes - examined the participants’ underlying beliefs regarding the impact of individual environmental behaviour. Results demonstrated that the majority of respondents considered their consumption choices to be highly influential, which aligns with Ajzen’s (1991) Theory of Planned Behaviour that suggests attitudes can predict behavioural intentions. Additionally, the findings support Grankvist and Biel’s (2007) assertion that individuals with pro-environmental attitudes tend to exhibit more sustainable purchase behaviours, underscoring the importance of fostering such attitudes in target consumers.

Lastly, the third theme, purchase behaviour, discussed the direct impact of green marketing strategies on consumer decisions. Results indicated that green marketing initiatives, such as eco-labelling and green advertising, had a significant positive influence on consumers’ willingness to adopt sustainable practices and support green products (Dangelico & Vocalelli, 2017). Moreover, the findings were consistent with the proposed hypothesis, which stated that consumers’ perception of green products and marketing practices positively affects their buying behaviour.


Discussion of Findings in Relation to the Literature Review and Limitations of Findings 
The findings from this research support and expand upon the existing literature on green marketing and its impact on consumer behaviour. As previously mentioned, the study identified three primary thematic codes through which green marketing strategies could influence consumer purchasing behaviour in the Nigerian manufacturing industry: green awareness, attitudes, and purchase behaviour.

In concurrence with the literature, green awareness emerged as a crucial factor driving consumer behaviour (Peattie & Crane, 2005). The results demonstrate the importance of developing targeted educational and promotional green campaigns aimed at increasing consumer awareness of sustainable practices and initiatives. This aligns with the findings of Alniacik et al. (2011) who emphasize the role of marketing communication in shaping consumer perceptions of green products while effectively bridging the ‘attitude-behaviour gap’.

The second theme - attitudes - supports the theoretical framework that was adopted for the study, Ajzen’s (1991) Theory of Planned Behaviour. According to this theory, a person’s attitude towards a behaviour plays a significant role in determining their behavioural intentions. By establishing a connection between pro-environmental attitudes and purchase behaviour, the findings echo the assertions of Grankvist and Biel (2007) while reinforcing the need to adopt strategies aimed at fostering favourable attitudes towards sustainability within the target audience.

Lastly, the theme of purchase behaviour captures the direct influence of green marketing strategies on consumers’ buying decisions. The significant positive influence of eco-labelling and green advertising on purchasing behaviour, as highlighted by this research, corroborates the findings of earlier studies conducted by Dangelico and Vocalelli (2017) and del Río-González (2005). These results signify the importance of crafting comprehensive green marketing campaigns that effectively inform and persuade consumers to opt for environmentally-friendly options.

Nevertheless, the study has some limitations that need to be recognized. First, the research employed a relatively small sample size, which may have an impact on the generalizability of the results. The findings represent the opinions and perceptions of a selected group and may not necessarily encapsulate the entire consumer audience in Nigeria’s manufacturing industry. Future research could consider a larger and more diverse sample, adding more validity to the findings and enhancing generalizability.

Second, the study solely focused on the Nigerian manufacturing industry, implying that the insights gained may not be applicable across various national contexts or industries. For a more thorough understanding of the scope and impact of green marketing strategies, it is essential to extend the research to other countries and sectors, allowing for cross-comparisons and a comprehensive understanding of consumer behaviour in various contexts.

Lastly, the present research focused primarily on the influence of green marketing strategies on consumers, without delving into the potential barriers to green consumption, such as cost-sensitive behaviour, lack of information access, and limited product availability. Future studies could investigate these inhibiting factors further and evaluate measures employed by organizations to overcome them.

Despite these limitations, the present study contributes significantly to the existing body of knowledge on green marketing and consumer behaviour, focusing on the insights from the Nigerian manufacturing industry.




CONCLUSION
The current research project sought to explore the impact of green marketing strategies on consumers’ buying behaviour in the Nigerian manufacturing industry. For this, the study evaluated  existing body of knowledge on green marketing strategies, consumer perception and awareness of green products, and the role of environmental concerns in consumer buying behaviour. The theoretical underpinning was derived from Ajzen’s (1991) Theory of Planned Behaviour, which emphasizes the significance of attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control in predicting behavioural intentions.

The research utilized a positivist paradigm, employing a descriptive and correlational research design to gather data through surveys and interviews with a stratified random sample from the Nigerian manufacturing industry. The findings revealed a significant positive relationship between green marketing strategies and consumer buying behaviour. Additionally, three influential factors were identified – green awareness, attitudes, and purchase behaviour – which aligned with the literature review and theoretical framework. The research also corroborated the hypothesis that consumers’ perception of green products and marketing practices positively affect their buying behaviour.

The implications of this research have both academic and practical relevance. Academically, the study enriches the existing literature on green marketing and consumer behaviour, particularly in the context of Nigeria’s manufacturing industry. It provides insight into the direct and indirect impact of green marketing strategies on consumer decisions and identifies potential avenues for future research. Practically, this research offers valuable implications for organizations in the manufacturing sector seeking to adopt sustainable practices while influencing consumer behaviour. The emphasis on green awareness highlights the need for effective communication and education strategies that can enhance consumers’ understanding of sustainability and motivate them to make eco-friendly choices. Similarly, fostering positive attitudes towards green practices and products by utilizing persuasive marketing techniques like eco-labelling and green advertising can significantly improve consumers’ buying behaviour.

However, it is essential to acknowledge the study’s limitations such as the relatively small sample size and the focus on a single industry within Nigerian manufacturing. Future research could address these limitations by employing a more extensive and diverse sample, as well as exploring different industries and geographical contexts. Additionally, future studies might explore barriers to green consumption and strategies undertaken by organizations to mitigate these challenges.

periodo se non appoggiandosi a partner esterni;
● · modificazioni della catena del valore: i mutamenti dei
bisogni dei clienti potrebbero far perdere valore ad alcune
attività della catena del valore su cui prima si fondava il
vantaggio competitivo, richiedendo all'azienda una rapida
ristrutturazione della catena stessa e l'attivazione di nuove
competenze.
● ·
innovazioni tecnologiche: può accadere che l'azienda
non sia in grado di impadronirsi delle tecnologie emergenti o
non sia in grado di rinnovare le proprie competenze nei tempi
richiesti dal mercato;
● · apertura di nuovi mercati: nei mercati emergenti e in
evoluzione l'integrazione tra imprese facilita la possibilità di
accedere a competenze nuove e diverse.
L’outsourcing strategico si evolve verso la filiera, assumendo la
configurazione di una vera e propria struttura organizzativa. I professionisti
delle risorse umane giocano un ruolo fondamentale nella gestione dei
processi di filiera, poiché si tratta di gestire indirettamente persone non legate
da contratti di lavoro. La filiera diventa una parte dell’azienda e raggiunge
dimensioni e specializzazioni tali da garantire costi e qualità, offrendo
competenze eccellenti anche alle piccole aziende. Tuttavia, la crescita interna
delle persone attraverso una varietà di funzioni ed esperienze viene meno.
Ciò richiede un ripensamento del ruolo della DRU, che si trova sempre più in
difficoltà a gestire rapporti di lavoro di tipo tradizionale.
Dal telelavoro al networkingLe tecnologie dell’informazione e della comunicazione (ICT) hanno permesso lo sviluppo di
nuove soluzioni per la gestione del lavoro e del controllo delle attività. Il telelavoro, definito
come il lavoro svolto a distanza con l’utilizzo delle ICT, rappresenta una delle innovazioni più
interessanti nell’organizzazione del lavoro.
Il telelavoro elimina le limitazioni della localizzazione fisica e rappresenta una prospettiva
evolutiva per il lavoro in rete nell’economia dell’informazione.
Il telelavoro si presenta in varie forme organizzative che dipendono da diversi fattori come gli
obiettivi degli attori coinvolti, le soluzioni tecnologiche adottate e la struttura tecnologica
disponibile.
Queste forme non rappresentano modalità alternative l’una all’altra, ma spesso convivono.
Le forme che stanno prevalendo sono un mix di lavoro svolto a distanza e in azienda, poiché
il telelavoro è estremamente flessibile e utilizza le tecnologie dell’informazione. Anche il
lavoro svolto al telefono può essere considerato telelavoro.
Lo sviluppo del telelavoro è legato alla rivoluzione digitale e ai cambiamenti nei modi di
produrre, comunicare e consumare. Anche nei settori tradizionali, l’ibridazione tra
tradizionale e digitale sta aprendo nuove prospettive. La popolazione è mal distribuita nel
territorio e ha problemi di mobilità, il che rende il telelavoro un’alternativa alla mobilità delle
persone.
Tuttavia, per lo sviluppo del lavoro online sono necessarie non solo connessioni veloci ed
economiche, ma anche soluzioni organizzative e competenze per trasformare il telelavoro in
una scelta strategica come nello smart working.
Passare da un lavoro organizzato in modo tradizionale a un altro articolato in una rete di
relazioni e scambi comporta una rivoluzione dei modi di essere e di operare delle
organizzazioni e dei lavoratori.
Le soluzioni organizzative del telelavoro sono molteplici e dipendono da diversi fattori, tra cui
gli obiettivi degli attori coinvolti, i problemi e le esigenze da soddisfare, le soluzioni tecniche
adottate e la struttura tecnologica disponibile.
Il telelavoro può essere un’opportunità per rimettere in circolo le zone marginali senza
stravolgimenti ambientali.
L'impresa può utilizzare il telelavoro, sostanzialmente secondo due modalità.
● · La prima consiste nello sfruttare le potenzialità di ricollocazione spazio-temporale
delle prestazioni lavorative (dilatazione del tempo e un annullamento o contrazione
dello spazio cioè delle distanze).
● · La seconda consiste in una dilatazione delle possibilità di accedere direttamente,
attraverso proprie interfacce organizzative, ai vantaggi di specializzazioniprofessionali e di servizi estremamente qualificati, come nel caso del crowdworking (vedi Scheda 10.5), Una terza modalità di uso del telelavoro, che implica un superamento dei suoi limiti e un impatto più profondo sull'organizzazione del lavoro, è il net.
Il networking è una modalità di lavoro che coinvolge più attori tramite interfacce tecnologiche per coordinarsi anche a distanza. Questo permette di gestire attività complesse con un elevato numero di attori e scambi informativi. L’uso strategico del networking richiede la progettazione di strumenti organizzativi per la condivisione della conoscenza. Per fare networking come ricollocazione spazio-temporale delle prestazioni lavorative, è necessario avere una tecnologia adeguata e individuare le interfacce più efficaci per supportare il coordinamento tra persone e organizzazioni remote.
Il cambiamento introdotto è ● · profondo nella strutturazione dei tempi (tempo di lavoro e tempo di non lavoro) e degli spazi (dove ubicare gli "uffici");
● · ma superficiale nella natura e nel contenuto dei processi operativi, la cui architettura può restare invariata
PAG 365-370 Il networking "non strategico" permette di colmare le inefficienza dovute alle difficoltà e ai costi di coordinamento, ma esauriti i margini di recupero smette di essere "appetibile". Il networking strategico non si limita a modificare profondamente la strutturazione dei tempi, ma richiede agli attori che lavorano in rete di "coordinare i loro tempi". Questo coordinamento può essere ● semplice se applicato ad attività sequenziali, ● più complesso quando gli attori devono agire congiuntamente dopo aver definito in autonomia le azioni da compiere
La time-based competition richiede di creare continuamente nuovi prodotti, in tempi rapidi e

Salut à toi, futur maître nageur de ta marque personnelle ! Dans ce chapitre, on va parler d’une petite bête qui se cache souvent dans le petit bassin de notre esprit : le syndrome de l’imposteur. Pas de panique ! Ensemble, on va apprendre à l’identifier, à faire la paix avec et à aller de l’avant. Alors, enfile ton bonnet et tes lunettes, c’est parti !

I. Le syndrome de l’imposteur : qu’est-ce que c’est ?

Plouf ! Le syndrome de l’imposteur, ou “impostor phenomenon” en anglais, est un sentiment d’illégitimité qui touche beaucoup de personnes, même les plus compétentes. C’est un peu comme si, malgré toutes nos compétences et nos expériences, on avait l’impression de ne pas mériter les succès que l’on obtient. On se sent alors comme un(e) apprenti(e) nageur(se), essayant de se débrouiller dans le grand bassin.

II. Comment l’identifier ?

On te teste avec un petit quizz ! Réponds sincèrement à ces questions : 
1. As-tu tendance à attribuer tes succès à la chance ou au hasard, et non à tes compétences et à ton travail ? 
2. Es-tu souvent en proie à la peur d’être démasqué(e) et que ton entourage se rende compte de ton “incompétence” ?
3. Te compares-tu constamment aux autres et te dis-tu que tu ne seras jamais à leur hauteur ?

Si tu as répondu “oui” à une ou plusieurs de ces questions, il est possible que le syndrome de l’imposteur joue au water polo dans ta tête. Mais pas de panique ! On va apprendre à l’apprivoiser ensemble.

III. Faire la paix avec l’imposteur : des tips pour surmonter ce sentiment

1. Prends conscience de la situation
D’abord, il faut bien identifier les moments où tu te sens submergé(e) par le sentiment de ne pas être légitime. Mets ces moments en lumière pour mieux les déchiffrer. Plus on est conscient de ce qui se passe sous l’eau, mieux notre nage sera efficace !

2. Partage-le avec d’autres
Parler de ce syndrome avec d’autres personnes peut être salvateur. Tu verras qu’il y a beaucoup d’autres nageurs sous la surface qui ressentent la même chose et ensemble, vous pourrez tenir la palme sur cet imposteur !

3. Fais le bilan de tes compétences et quali-plouf-cations
Liste tout ce que tu sais faire, tes diplômes, tes expériences et les félicitations que tu as reçues. Tu verras que tu as déjà beaucoup nager et que tu as beaucoup de raisons d’être fier(e) de toi.

4. Des jeux de rôle pour lutter contre l’imposteur à domicile !
Il est temps de mettre ton imposteur à l’épreuve : demande à un proche de jouer le rôle du recruteur ou d’un(e) collègue et d’avoir une conversation où tu devras vendre ton “produit” (toi !). Cela t’aidera à prendre conscience de ta valeur et à trouver des arguments pour te défendre face à cet imposteur.

Maintenant que tu as différentes techniques pour te rapprocher de ton syndrome de l’imposteur et le dépasser, sache que tu as déjà fait un grand plongeon vers la cohérence entre toi-même et le regard que tu portes sur tes compétences. Continuons de propulser cette marque personnelle ! Surtout, ne te laisse pas couler par cette petite voix qui te dit que tu ne fais pas le poids. Au contraire, nage avec force dans cette piscine du personal branding !

pourquoi la gamification, le pas de côté et le jeu sont essentiels pour aborder des sujets graves comme l’orientation ?
La gamification, le pas de côté et le jeu sont essentiels pour aborder des sujets graves comme l’orientation pour plusieurs raisons :

1. Diminuer le stress et l’anxiété : L’orientation et la prise de décisions concernant son futur professionnel peuvent être sources de stress et d’anxiété pour de nombreuses personnes. La gamification et le jeu permettent d’aborder ces sujets sous un angle plus léger et amusant, ce qui contribue à réduire le sentiment de pression.

2. Encourager la créativité : Introduire des éléments ludiques dans l’apprentissage et la réflexion permet de stimuler la créativité et d’ouvrir l’esprit à de nouvelles idées et perspectives. Cette approche peut aider à explorer des options d’orientation auxquelles on n’aurait pas pensé auparavant.

3. Faciliter l’engagement : Un environnement de jeu est généralement plus engageant et motivant, ce qui incite les participants à s’impliquer davantage et à être proactifs dans leur réflexion sur l’orientation. Un participant actif sera plus enclin à prendre des décisions éclairées.

4. Améliorer les compétences sociales : Les jeux et la gamification encouragent souvent la collaboration, la communication et le travail d’équipe. En abordant l’orientation sous cet angle, on peut développer ces compétences sociales tout en réfléchissant à son futur professionnel.

5. Développer la prise de risque : Le jeu permet de se confronter à des situations inédites et d’apprendre à prendre des décisions sans craindre l’échec. Cela favorise la prise de risque et l’autonomie dans le processus d’orientation.

6. Favoriser l’autoréflexion : Le pas de côté offre une distance permettant de prendre du recul et d’observer sa situation de manière plus objective. Cette distance permet de mieux se connaître, d’identifier ses forces et ses faiblesses, et de prendre des décisions d’orientation alignées avec ses aspirations et ses valeurs.

En somme, la gamification, le pas de côté et le jeu sont essentiels pour aborder des sujets graves comme l’orientation, car ils créent un environnement propice à l’apprentissage, à la réflexion, à la créativité et au développement personnel. Ils permettent de mieux se connaître et de prendre des décisions plus éclairées, tout en réduisant la pression et le stress souvent associés à ces enjeux. »

Potential Approaches to Overcome Human Resource Challenges in Green Air
In the context of GA’s current situation, some core HRM concepts and contemporary practices that can be critically assessed include employee motivation theories, stakeholder theory, workforce diversity and inclusion, recruitment and hiring strategies, and employee engagement and well-being.
One aspect of motivation theories that can be applied to GA’s problems is the expectancy theory by Fudge and Schlacter (1999). This theory suggests that employees are driven to act in a certain way based on the expectation that their efforts will lead to a desired outcome, and this outcome will be rewarding. In the case of GA, the company can use the expectancy theory to increase the motivation of employees by clarifying expectations and establishing a strong connection between individual and organizational goals. This approach may help GA to temporarily maintain employee motivation while they work on improving the compensation packages.
Another core HRM concept relevant to GA’s situation is stakeholder theory, which highlights the need for organizations to manage relationships with various stakeholders effectively (Thornock, 2016). In GA’s case, the relationship with trade unions has been challenging due to conflicts over pay and working conditions. These tensions could have been better managed through a more proactive approach to communication, negotiation, and conflict resolution involving all relevant stakeholders.
The concept of diversity and inclusion in the workplace is also critical for GA. Due to the mixed fleet crews, employees with different levels of experience, contracts, and backgrounds are working together, which could lead to conflicts or misunderstandings. It is essential for GA to foster an inclusive work environment that acknowledges and accommodates employees’ differences while promoting a sense of belonging and collaboration.
A relevant contemporary HR practice for GA is developing a strong recruitment and hiring strategy. As GA faces potential workforce shortages, they will need a comprehensive plan to attract and retain qualified employees with skills that match the organization’s needs. This recruitment strategy could include targeted job postings, campus hiring, increased employee referrals, and the use of technology such as social media and online job portals. GA could also consider offering competitive training programs and development opportunities to entice prospective employees.
Finally, employee engagement and well-being should be a top priority for GA’s HR team. The current low morale and dissatisfaction among employees is affecting the quality of service provided to customers, further damaging the company’s public image. GA needs to engage its employees by addressing their concerns, providing support, and creating an environment that promotes a healthy work-life balance. Such efforts can improve employee satisfaction, increase productivity, and thus boost the organization’s overall performance.
In sum, GA’s HR team should critically assess and implement appropriate HRM concepts and contemporary practices to address the critical issues of employee motivation, stakeholder relations, workforce diversity and inclusion, recruitment and hiring, and employee engagement and well-being. By proactively addressing these challenges, GA can create a positive work environment that ultimately leads to improved organizational performance and customer satisfaction.

Recommended Solutions
In light of the aforementioned HR issues faced by GA, several recommended solutions can be proposed to help the airline address its current challenges, improve employee morale, and strengthen its public image.
First and foremost, GA should consider engaging in open and transparent dialogue with its employees and the trade unions representing them. Maintaining strong communication channels, actively listening to employees’ concerns, and being transparent about the organization’s goals and challenges can help build trust and facilitate constructive negotiations (Baraldi and Radaelli, 2020). Collaborative problem-solving efforts with trade unions can lead to mutually beneficial agreements on issues such as pay, working conditions, and employment contracts, ultimately fostering a positive work environment.
Revisiting GA’s compensation packages is another solution that merits consideration. While the current financial situation may prevent immediate changes to employee compensation, GA could develop a comprehensive plan outlining adjustments to be made once the organization’s financial health improves (Purcell and Hutchinson, 2007). This strategy may include offering more competitive salaries or restoring some of the benefits and rewards that employees previously enjoyed. By presenting a well-defined plan for the future, GA can regain its employees’ trust and reinforce commitment to the organization.
Additionally, GA should consider implementing measures that promote employee engagement and overall well-being. This may involve offering greater flexibility with working hours, ensuring that employees have a healthy work-life balance, and providing resources for mental and physical health support (Kahn, 1990). By fostering a supportive work environment, GA can improve employee morale, reduce absenteeism, and enhance productivity.
To address the potential workforce shortage and recruitment challenges, GA needs to develop a strategic approach to recruiting and retaining talent. Armstrong and Taylor (2020) suggest adopting a multifaceted recruitment strategy that incorporates targeted job postings, partnerships with educational institutions, employee referral programs, and the utilization of social media and online platforms. Additionally, offering continuous learning, development, and growth opportunities within the organization can make GA a more attractive employer, ultimately aiding in the recruitment of new employees.
Lastly, GA should strive to improve its public perception by delivering exceptional customer service and addressing customer complaints efficiently. To achieve this goal, the organization must invest in training and development programs aimed at enhancing employees’ customer service skills (Zeithaml et al., 2006). Empowered and motivated employees are more likely to contribute to an improved customer experience which, in turn, can positively impact GA’s public image.
In conclusion, by implementing these recommendations, GA can address its HR challenges, improve employee morale, and enhance its public reputation, paving the way for organizational success and growth in an increasingly competitive market.

Conclusion
In conclusion, the challenges faced by GA highlight the critical role of effective human resource management in maintaining employee satisfaction, fostering a positive work environment, and sustaining a competitive edge. Through open communication and collaboration with trade unions, revisiting compensation plans, promoting employee engagement and well-being, adopting strategic recruitment approaches, and investing in customer service training, GA can address the multifaceted issues that currently affect the organization. By proactively tackling these challenges and prioritizing the well-being and satisfaction of its employees, GA can pave the way for success in an increasingly competitive market while enhancing its public image and solidifying its position as a leading global airline.

Benim sana vereceğim veriler ile bu yazım tarzına uygun bana bir giriş yazar mısın? civanperçemi, kayışkıran, altınbaşak maydanoz, tarla atkuyruğu gibi diüretik bitkiler ile alakalı yazacağım. 
örnek almanı istediğim giriş:
Bitkilerin gıda olarak kullanılması yiyecek bulma çabasına eşlik eden deneme
yanılma ve öğrenme süreci ile gelişmiş ve bu süreçten en çok etkilenen sistemlerden biri
de sindirim sistemi olmuştur (Hoffmann, 2003). Sindirim oldukça kompleks bir olaydır
ve vegetatif sinir sistemi ile oldukça yakın bir ilişki içerisindedir (Zeybek ve Özgüç ,
2019). Bitkiler ile sindirim sistemi arasındaki ilişkinin sadece tüketilen bitkilerin
metabolizasyonu ile sınırlı olmadığı, aynı zamanda sindirim organlarını ve sindirim
kanallarını direkt etkiledikleri bilinmektedir (Hoffmann, 2003). M.Ö. 1550 yıllarına ait
olduğu bilinen Ebers papürüslerinde, 877 tane bitki reçetesi bulunduğu kayıtlıdır (Zeybek
ve Haksel, 2011). Günümüzde de sindirim sistemi rahatsızlıklarında etkisi olduğunu
bildiğimiz Thymus sp. (Kekik) , Carum carvi L. ( Kimyon) , Pimpinella anisum L.
( Anason), Chelidonium majus L. ( Kırlangıç otu ) gibi tıbbi ve aromatik bitkiler bitki
reçetelerinin içinde sıklıkla yer almışlardır (Baytop, 1999; Zeybek ve Haksel, 2010,
Zeybek ve Özgüç , 2019).). Oluşan bu bilgi birikimleri zamanla geliştirilmiş ve nesilden
nesile aktarılarak bugünlere kadar gelmiştir (Akalın, 1993). Türkiye’deki etnofarmasötik
botanik çalışmalara baktığımızda, bitkisel halk ilaçlarının da sindirim sistemi
rahatsızlıklarında yoğunlukla kullanıldığını görülmektedir (Koçyiğit ve Özhatay, 2006;
Akalın, 1993).
Bu çalışmada ele alınan, ESCOP ve diğer Monograf tıbbi ve aromatik bitkilerinin
seçimlerinde, fitoterapi sertifikasına sahip hekimlerin yönlendirmiş olduğu hastaların
eczanelerde tıbbi çay ve aromaterapötik ürünler üzerinde danışmanlık aldıkları
fitoterapötikler ve gıda takviyesi ürünleri ön planda tutulmuştur.

Crea flashcards del tipo domanda-risposta e parola-definizione: Gli approcci al job design Si sta attualmente revisionando il modello taylorista di organizzazione del lavoro, focalizzato sull'efficienza tramite la specializzazione dei lavoratori, la supervisione e gli incentivi basati sulla produttività. È necessaria un'analisi dei principi originali, degli approcci alternativi motivazionali e degli sviluppi successivi verso un approccio integrato. Questo processo di revisione non è ancora concluso.
L'approccio taylorista Secondo l'approccio taylorista, la divisione del lavoro può essere spinta fino al limite della divisibilità tecnica e delle dimensioni del mercato.
Tuttavia, la parcellizzazione delle mansioni comporta costi che non erano considerati dal taylorismo classico. Questi costi possono essere ridotti attraverso l'uso di strumenti di ristrutturazione del lavoro che consentono di ridefinire il grado di divisione del lavoro, dando vita all'approccio neo-taylorista.
L'approccio neo-taylorista si differenzia dal taylorismo classico per l'attenzione ai costi associati alla divisione del lavoro e alla generazione di economie di apprendimento e replicazione.
Più semplice è il compito, più volte viene ripetuto e più facilmente viene appreso. In questo
modo, la ripartizione delle mansioni tra più operatori può portare a un aumento della produttività complessiva. Tuttavia, la specializzazione e la ripetitività delle attività possono avere un impatto negativo sulla motivazione dei lavoratori. In generale, la revisione dei principi tayloristici è orientata verso l'integrazione di un approccio motivazionale alla progettazione del lavoro, che tiene conto delle esigenze dei lavoratori e del loro coinvolgimento nella definizione delle attività da svolgere.
L'approccio taylorista spinge la divisione del lavoro fino al limite della divisibilità tecnica e del mercato, ma comporta costi non considerati. L'approccio neo-taylorista cerca di ridurre questi costi attraverso la ristrutturazione del lavoro, dando importanza ai costi associati alla divisione del lavoro e alla generazione di economie di apprendimento e replicazione. Tuttavia, la specializzazione e la ripetitività delle attività possono influire negativamente sulla motivazione dei lavoratori.Pertanto, la revisione dei principi tayloristici mira all'integrazione di un approccio
motivazionale alla progettazione del lavoro, che consideri le esigenze dei lavoratori e il loro
coinvolgimento nella definizione delle attività.
Il taylorismo prevedeva la massima divisione del lavoro per ottenere il massimo profitto.
Tuttavia, questa divisione può generare costi di apprendimento ricorrenti, quando il
lavoratore deve riadattarsi a cambiamenti nella tecnologia, aumentando i tempi di
riapprendimento e riducendo la produttività.
L'approccio neo-taylorista tiene conto di questi costi e prevede la progettazione di mansioni
più varie e autonome, come il job enlargement, il job enrichment e il job rotation, per ridurre i
costi di coordinamento e supervisione.
Questa riorganizzazione potrebbe comportare un aumento dei costi di apprendimento
iniziale ma diminuire i costi di comportamento. In questo modo, il lavoratore, facendo leva
sulla varietà delle conoscenze e su una consapevolezza più completa del processo
produttivo, sarà in grado di tornare più rapidamente ai livelli di produttività attesi.
La spinta verso organizzazioni più orizzontali si basa su argomenti strutturali piuttosto che
comportamentali.
Ciò è dimostrato da un'antica storiella che descrive una gara di canoa tra un equipaggio
italiano e uno giapponese.
Gli italiani avevano sette comandanti e un rematore, mentre i giapponesi avevano un
comandante e sette rematori. I giapponesi vinsero, così gli italiani ingaggiarono una società
di consulenza americana che consigliò di avere quattro comandanti, due supervisori dei
comandanti, un capo dei supervisori e uno ai remi.
Tuttavia, nella successiva gara, i giapponesi vinsero ancora di più.
La morale della storia è che la gerarchia eccessiva non sempre porta al successo. Invece, le
organizzazioni orizzontali, in cui le decisioni sono prese in modo più democratico, possono
essere più efficaci.
e organizzazioni tendono a moltiplicare posti, funzioni e organi, perciò il movimento di
ristrutturazione del lavoro si accompagna alla reingegnerizzazione dei processi.
Il Bpr (Business Process Reengineering) prevede il ridisegno delle attività aziendali per
generare valore per il cliente interno ed esterno, ma a volte viene contrapposto al lean
thinking, che è un approccio meno tecnico e più pervasivo e mira alla progettazione e
riprogettazione a lungo termine dell'organizzazione del lavoro.
Parkinson stimava un tasso del 5-7% di crescita annua di posizioni inutili, ma questo valore
è probabilmente sopravvalutato.
L'approccio motivazionale
L'approccio motivazionale all'organizzazione del lavoro supera l'approccio neo-tayloristico,
vedendo il lavoratore come portatore di bisogni emotivi e sociali, oltre a quelli economici.
La varietà del lavoro, l'autonomia e la responsabilità consentono al lavoratore di identificarsi
nel ruolo che gli è assegnato, generando soddisfazione e utilità. Il contenuto del compito
diventa una ricompensa intrinseca poiché soddisfa il bisogno di achievement del lavoratore
e si realizza attraverso i feedback dell'attività svolta.
Questo approccio considera la motivazione del lavoratore come un fattore chiave per il
successo dell'organizzazione e quindi sottolinea l'importanza di progettare le attività
lavorative in modo tale da soddisfare le esigenze del lavoratore. In questo modo, il lavoro
non è solo un modo per guadagnare denaro, ma diventa anche una fonte di soddisfazionepersonale e di realizzazione, migliorando la qualità della vita del lavoratore e la produttività
dell'organizzazione.
Le ricompense intrinseche sono specifiche e stabili, diverse dalle ricompense estrinseche
come la retribuzione monetaria.
La motivazione al lavoro può creare soddisfazione per i lavoratori, i clienti e l'azienda stessa.
Tuttavia, molte aziende non danno abbastanza importanza a questa dimensione del
comportamento lavorativo. Un'azienda di servizi, ad esempio, si presenta ai potenziali clienti
come impiegatrice di personale preparato e motivato, dimostrando che la motivazione è un
elemento di differenziazione del servizio. La reattività alle ricompense intrinseche può
variare da individuo a individuo a seconda del sistema motivazionale di ciascuno.
